duckgpt_q9.json:
The EU AI Act uses a risk-based approach:

Unacceptable-risk AI is banned, including certain manipulative systems, social scoring, and some biometric uses.
High-risk AI has the toughest compliance duties, such as risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy/cybersecurity controls.
Limited-risk AI mainly has transparency duties, like telling users when they're interacting with AI or when content is AI-generated.
General-purpose AI (GPAI) models have their own rules for documentation, transparency, and copyright compliance.
Lower-risk AI is mostly unregulated beyond existing law and voluntary practices. 
European Union 1

Timing-wise, the Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies in phases: bans and AI literacy rules started on 2 February 2025; GPAI governance rules started on 2 August 2025; the main transparency and GPAI enforcement provisions started on 2 August 2026; and the high-risk rules now apply later for most systems — 2 December 2027 for certain stand-alone high-risk uses and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI built into regulated products.

The research shows no significant difference in weight loss between intermittent fasting and daily calorie restriction in most cases — with a notable recent exception.

When total calories are matched between the two approaches, intermittent fasting produces nearly identical weight loss to continuous daily calorie restriction. A major 2026 Cochrane review examined 22 randomized controlled trials with nearly 2,000 participants and found the weight loss difference between the two methods was "statistically indistinguishable from zero." [Rutgers University] A 2025 meta-analysis of 20 studies reached the same conclusion: intermittent fasting is not superior to calorie restriction for weight loss when calories are equal. [ScienceDirect]

A 2025 study published in Annals of Internal Medicine found that a 4:3 intermittent fasting approach (eating freely 4 days per week, restricting calories heavily on 3 days) produced greater weight loss than daily calorie restriction: 7.6% average weight loss versus 5% in the continuous restriction group. [cuanschutz.edu]

The researchers designed both groups to have identical weekly calorie deficits (34%), yet the 4:3 pattern still outperformed. [cuanschutz.edu]

The Cochrane review noted that current evidence provides little information about whether one method is easier to maintain than the other. Some people find intermittent fasting psychologically easier because they don't count calories daily, while others experience higher hunger levels during fasting windows. [ScienceDirect]1

When weight loss does occur with either method, both approaches show similar improvements in blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar control. The 4:3 intermittent fasting study did show slightly more favorable changes in these cardiometabolic markers, though researchers noted these were secondary outcomes requiring larger studies for confirmation. [cuanschutz.edu]
